concept_panel.title: Docker Images and Containers
concept_panel.explanation: A Dockerfile describes how to build an image. An image packages the application filesystem and metadata, while a container is a running instance of that image. Good Docker usage makes runtime dependencies explicit and reproducible. If a container depends on undeclared host files, the image is not self-contained.
key_takeaways: A container runs from an image.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand reproducible deployment artifacts.
concept_panel.practical_example: Copy requirements.txt, install dependencies, then copy app code to improve layer caching.

questions.prompt: Order a basic Docker image build flow.
questions.explanation: Copying dependency manifests before app code improves layer caching and makes builds faster.

questions.prompt: The same code needs different database URLs in dev and prod. Where should this differ?
questions.explanation: Environment variables separate runtime configuration from code and avoid rebuilding for each environment.

concept_panel.title: Runtime Configuration
concept_panel.explanation: Runtime configuration changes between environments without changing code. Database URLs, feature switches, API endpoints, and secrets should be injected through environment or secret management rather than hardcoded. This makes the same build artifact usable in dev, test, and production. Configuration discipline reduces accidental production mistakes.
key_takeaways: Code should not hardcode deployment-specific values.
Secrets need secret handling, not source control.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand deployable software configuration.
concept_panel.practical_example: Set `DATABASE_URL` differently in local development and production deployment.

questions.explanation: CI validates a change before CD deploys the exact built artifact.

concept_panel.title: CI/CD Pipelines
concept_panel.explanation: CI validates changes automatically with tests, type checks, and builds. CD deploys a validated artifact to an environment. The important principle is that the artifact you deploy should be traceable to the code that passed checks. Deployment health checks and rollbacks limit blast radius when a bad version escapes.
key_takeaways: CI catches broken changes before merge/deploy.
CD should deploy a known artifact.
Health checks and rollback make releases safer.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand deployment safety and operational traceability.
concept_panel.practical_example: A pipeline installs dependencies, runs tests, builds an artifact, then deploys it with health checks.

questions.prompt: A deployment passes build but fails its health check. What should happen?
questions.explanation: Health checks are deployment gates. Failed health should prevent bad versions from spreading.

concept_panel.title: Deployment Safety
concept_panel.explanation: Deployment safety limits blast radius and makes failure reversible. Health checks stop bad releases, canaries expose changes to limited traffic, feature flags decouple deployment from release, and rollbacks return to a known-good version. The important idea is proving the new version works before trusting it with all traffic.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand production release risk.
concept_panel.practical_example: Deploy to 5 percent of traffic, watch errors and latency, then continue or roll back.

questions.explanation: Release safety is about limiting blast radius and making bad changes reversible.

questions.prompt: A secret API key is committed into source control. What is the issue?
questions.explanation: Secrets should not live in source. Use environment configuration or secret storage and rotate exposed keys.
options: Secret leakage; move it to secret management/env config
questions.answer: Secret leakage; move it to secret management/env config

concept_panel.title: Secret Management
concept_panel.explanation: Secrets are credentials such as API keys, database passwords, and signing keys. They should not be committed to source control because repository history is hard to erase and access is broad. Use environment-backed secret stores or local ignored files, and rotate leaked secrets. Treat secrets as operational risk.
key_takeaways: Never commit secrets to source control.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand operational security basics.
concept_panel.practical_example: Move a committed API key into a secret store and revoke the old key.

questions.prompt: Which outputs help diagnose a production deploy?
questions.explanation: Deploy diagnosis needs version provenance, runtime health, and logs tied to the release.

concept_panel.title: Logs, Metrics, and Traces
concept_panel.explanation: Observability gives evidence about production behavior. Logs explain specific events, metrics show trends and rates, and traces follow one request across services. Good incident answers use these signals to narrow the problem instead of guessing. Observability should be designed before the system is failing.
key_takeaways: Metrics reveal trends, rates, and percentiles.
Traces expose cross-service latency and failures.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can debug production systems with evidence.
concept_panel.practical_example: A slow checkout trace can show that inventory, not payments, dominates latency.

questions.prompt: A bug appears only after deployment, but the built artifact is not recorded. What practice is missing?
questions.explanation: You need to know exactly what code and build artifact is running to debug or roll back confidently.

concept_panel.title: Build Artifact Traceability
concept_panel.explanation: A deployable artifact should be tied to the commit, checks, and environment that produced it. Without artifact traceability, debugging and rollback become guesswork. CI/CD pipelines should deploy the same artifact that passed validation. This is especially important when a bug appears only after deployment.
key_takeaways: Know exactly what version is running.
Deploy the artifact that passed checks.
Traceability makes rollback and debugging reliable.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand release provenance and production debugging.
concept_panel.practical_example: Attach commit SHA and build ID to every deployed release and log them at startup.

questions.prompt: A container works on one machine because it depends on a file outside the image. What is broken?
questions.explanation: Container images should include declared runtime dependencies so they run consistently across machines.
